doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Difficulty of SuperSax Bird transcriptions and Med Flory's writing
summary: On playing Koko, he discusses the hard inner parts, Med's writing, the group's history and its decline.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay, one more little finger buster here.
You know which album this is from?
Oh this is where Med sings. Does Med sing on this?
Yeah, I don’t think I got that far. That is just I mean outrageous.

It is. I’ll tell you, of course Med always wants to kill me. Med or Nimitz want to kill me when I say this but the lead part or the baritone part are the easiest parts. The second alto and the two tenor parts are just a bear. And if I’d known you were going to do that I’d have brought you a copy of the second alto part. In fact, maybe I’ll send it to you.
I’d love it. Because I know what you’re saying because all those lower harmonies and stuff, and when they write the arrangements they’re not necessarily taking into account —

Med does. Med does all the writing. Well he did, Buddy Clark did some and Warne Marsh did some. Med never writes a repeated note, and for some reason he doesn’t use too many scales. I don’t know why he doesn’t do that because they’re usually kind of easy to voice and to play on. Or diminished chords. But even with that, I mean in other words he’ll cross voice, rather than repeat a note. But they’re still hard, they’re really hard.
How much time would you have to get that ready?

Well I wasn’t on the original SuperSax. It was Bill Perkins first and then Joe Lopes, the first couple of years. They spent a year rehearsing in Perk’s garage before they even ventured outside. But see the band doesn’t work anymore, that’s the trouble. So Med’s got a band, a big band, with seven or eight brass and the sax is SuperSax in front, and then the L.A. voices too. Well that’s like a 19-piece band, and it’s hard to even book a trio in this town let alone a 19 piece band. So he’s put all his effort into that for the last © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

several years. As a result SuperSax is not working, not doing anything. When we were working quite a bit, even three or four times a month, this stuff was easy. But I mean well it was not easy but everyone had it under their fingers, even the inner parts. But you know we’ll get a gig now and Med will call maybe a three-hour rehearsal and we’ll go over some of these things, but you can’t begin to get all those things. I mean it’s not only this, there’s a whole host of those things that are really very difficult. Even the slow ones are hard.
Even the slow ones. Some of the ballads, “Lover Man” is impossible, only because the saxes have to lay behind the time so far, like Bird did. “Embraceable You.”
Yeah. So it’s not just a finger thing, it’s a whole concept of where’s the time.
And if you don’t know Bird, it’s just — you know you really have to know Bird to play that, to know the way he played it.
